question: For a synthetic adult with cancer weighing 60 kg, without known renal failure, major edema, or refeeding risk, what approximate daily energy and protein targets are reasonable when individualized calorimetry is unavailable? Show the calculation and explain its limits.

cards.description: Weight loss, intake, BMI, muscle function, and nutrition assessment
cards.summary: Track intake, weight trajectory, and BMI from diagnosis. An abnormal screen warrants assessment of symptoms, muscle, function, and inflammation. Normal BMI does not exclude clinically important nutritional deterioration.

cards.description: General adult energy and protein targets and their limitations
cards.summary: When individualized measurement is unavailable, estimate 25-30 kcal/kg/day. Protein should exceed 1 g/kg/day and, when feasible, approach 1.5 g/kg/day. These are adjustable estimates, not initial refeeding rates.

cards.description: Inadequate oral intake, dysphagia, mucositis, and a functioning gut
cards.summary: Escalate from counseling and oral supplements to enteral support when intake remains inadequate. PN becomes relevant when enteral support is infeasible or insufficient. Treat symptoms and assess swallowing safety.

cards.description: Intestinal failure, obstruction, PN burdens, prognosis, and goals
cards.locator: ESMO nutrition-support sections; ASCO nutritional recommendation 1.2
cards.summary: Intestinal failure can justify considering PN in selected patients; cachexia alone does not justify routine PN. Assess reversible causes, performance, anticipated benefit, prognosis, goals, and burdens. Comfort and symptom relief take priority near death; PN decisions require specialist discussion.

cards.description: Multifactorial wasting, counseling, and updated appetite-drug evidence
cards.locator: ASCO 2020 recommendations 1.1-1.2; ASCO 2023 recommendations 2.1-2.2; ESMO assessment
cards.summary: Cachexia involves disease-related metabolic changes and muscle loss, not simply low intake. Offer individualized dietitian input, nutrient-dense food, symptom care, and realistic goals. Routine tubes or PN are not established treatments for advanced-cancer cachexia alone. ASCO's 2023 update permits selected clinician-supervised low-dose olanzapine for appetite/weight; the supporting populations were mainly lung/GI cancers.

cards.description: High-risk nutrition restart, thiamine, electrolytes, and monitoring
cards.summary: BMI below 16 or low baseline phosphate, potassium, or magnesium indicates high refeeding risk. Use expert-supervised cautious initiation; NICE suggests at most 10 kcal/kg/day initially, with 5 in extreme cases, then gradual increase. Give thiamine before and during early feeding, replace electrolytes as needed, and monitor fluids, glucose, phosphate, magnesium, and potassium. Do not start full maintenance targets immediately. Rate and correction decisions require local clinical protocols.

cards.description: Neutropenia, unnecessary dietary restriction, and food hygiene
cards.locator: ASCO 2022 dietary recommendations; NCI reducing foodborne illness
cards.summary: A routinely restrictive neutropenic diet has not shown infection-prevention benefit and is not recommended by ASCO for that purpose. Emphasize hygiene, safe storage and cooking, and avoidance of unsafe raw/undercooked or unpasteurized products. Follow specific transplant-center protocols where applicable while protecting nutritional intake.

cards.description: High-dose vitamins/antioxidants, deficiency correction, and interactions
cards.summary: Use ordinary micronutrient intake rather than high doses without a demonstrated deficiency. Antioxidant supplements can interact with treatment, and safety/benefit evidence is uncertain. Review the exact products with the oncology team; food-based nutrition and clinician-directed deficiency correction are distinct from megadose supplementation.

cards.description: Pancreatic cancer, malabsorption, steatorrhea, and enzyme replacement
cards.summary: NICE recommends enteric-coated pancreatin for unresectable pancreatic cancer. Weight loss with greasy stools should prompt assessment of maldigestion and other causes, not only calorie advice. Enzyme selection, meal-time use, titration, and nutritional follow-up require the treating team; the source recommendation does not specify a universal dose.

cards.description: Fasting or ketogenic diets during treatment in a person losing weight
cards.locator: ESPEN recommendation 8; ASCO 2022 dietary evidence review
cards.summary: Avoid energy-restrictive diets in malnourished or at-risk patients. Evidence does not establish fasting or ketogenic diets as routine cancer-treatment adjuncts. Prioritize adequate intake and explain uncertainty without claiming diet cures cancer.

sources.title: Metabolic response to enteral food in different phases of cancer cachexia in rats.
sources.authors: Z Zylicz, O Schwantje, D J Wagener, H T Folgering
sources.abstract: The resting energy expenditure (REE) and postprandial energy expenditure (PPEE) were measured using closed-circuit indirect calorimetry in Walker 256 carcinosarcoma-bearing rats. The results were compared to the appropriate controls. The PPEE measurements were performed after oral test feeding. At the beginning of the tumor growth, the REE and PPEE were similar in all groups. In the second week, the tumor-bearing rats showed increased REE and decreased PPEE. The tumor-bearing rats lost weight and became anorectic. After day 14, the REE rapidly dropped to very low values and the body weight continued to decrease. This study makes it possible to differentiate three phases of cancer cachexia: silent or preclinical, hypermetabolic and hypometabolic.

sources.title: Cancer cachexia: measured and predicted resting energy expenditures for nutritional needs evaluation.
sources.authors: Gyasi Johnson, Agnès Sallé, Gérard Lorimier, Laurent Laccourreye, Bernard Enon, Vincent Blin, Yann Jousset, Jean-Pierre Arnaud, Yves Malthièry, Gilles Simard, Patrick Ritz
sources.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Cancer cachexia is associated with weight loss, poor nutritional status, and systemic inflammation. Accurate nutritional support for patients is calculated on resting energy expenditure (REE) measurement or prediction. The present study evaluated the agreement between measured and predicted REE (mREE and pREE, respectively) and the influence of acute phase response (APR) on REE.
METHODS: Thirty-six patients with cancer were divided into weight-stable (WS; weight loss <2%) and weight-losing (WL; weight loss >5%) patients. Measured REE was measured by indirect calorimetry and adjusted for fat-free mass (FFM). The Bland-Altman approach was used to assess the agreement between mREE and pREE from the Harris-Benedict equations (HBE). Blood levels of C-reactive protein were assessed.
RESULTS: There was no difference in mREE between groups (WS 1677 +/- 273, WL 1521 +/- 305) even when mREE was adjusted for FFM (WS 1609 +/- 53, WL 1589 +/- 53). In WL patients, FFM-adjusted REE correlated with blood C-reactive protein levels (r = 0.471, P = 0.048). HBEs tend to underestimate REE in both groups.
CONCLUSION: WL and WS patients with cancer had similar REEs but were different in terms of APR. APR could contribute to weight loss through enhancing REE. In a clinical context, HBE was in poor agreement with mREE in both groups.

sources.title: Resting energy expenditure and body composition in patients with newly detected cancer.
sources.authors: Dong-xing Cao, Guo-hao Wu, Bo Zhang, Ying-jun Quan, Jia Wei, Huan Jin, Yi Jiang, Zi-ang Yang
sources.abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Elevated resting energy expenditure (REE) may be a major determinant in the development of cancer cachexia. The aim of the study was to evaluate REE and body composition in cancer patients and find out the relationship between energy expenditure and substrate utilization.
METHODS: Measured resting energy expenditure (mREE), carbohydrate oxidation (C-O), and fat oxidation (F-O) were measured by indirect calorimetry in 714 cancer patients and 642 controls. Extracellular fluid (ECF), intracellular fluid (ICF), and total water (TW) were measured by bioelectrical impedance appliance; fat mass (FM), fat free mass (FFM), and body cell mass (BCM) were further determined.
RESULTS: Compared with the controls, cancer patients showed no significant difference in mREE, but had higher mREE/FFM and mREE/pREE. 46.7% (n=333) of cancer patients were hypermetabolic, 43.5% (n=310) normometabolic, and 9.8% (n=71) hypometabolic; whereas 25.2% (n=162) of control subjects were hypermetabolic, 56.5% (n=363) normometabolic, and 18.3% (n=117) hypometabolic. Cancer patients showed an increase in F-O, ECF, TW/BW and ECF/BW; and a decrease in C-O, npRQ, ICF, ICF/BW. REE was correlated to substrate oxidation rate. Cancer patients exhibited an elevation in FM, FM/BW, FFM, and BCM, and a decrease in FFM/BW.
CONCLUSIONS: 1. Cancer patients had elevated REE. Cancer type, pathological stage and duration of disease influenced REE. 2. Aberrations in substrate utilization may contribute to the elevated REE in cancer patients. 3. FM, FFM, and BCM diminished in cancer patients, which may be related to the elevated REE.

sources.title: Resting energy expenditure in the risk assessment of anticancer treatments.
sources.authors: Anne Jouinot, Clara Vazeille, Jean Philippe Durand, Olivier Huillard, Pascaline Boudou-Rouquette, Romain Coriat, Jeanne Chapron, Nathalie Neveux, Jean Pascal De Bandt, Jerome Alexandre, Luc Cynober, Francois Goldwasser
sources.abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Alterations of nutritional and performance status (PS) are associated with higher risk of chemotherapy toxicity. Increased resting energy expenditure (REE) is frequent in cancer patients and may contribute to cachexia. We investigated whether abnormal energetic metabolism could predict early acute limiting toxicities (ELT) of anticancer treatments.
METHODS: In this observational monocentric study, REE was measured by indirect calorimetry before treatment initiation. Based on the ratio of measured REE to REE predicted by the Harris-Benedict formula, patients were classified as hypometabolic (<90%), normometabolic (90-110%) or hypermetabolic (>110%). Body mass index, weight loss, PS, albumin, transthyretin, C-reactive protein (CRP) and muscle mass (CT-scan) were studied. Were defined as ELT any unplanned hospitalization or any adverse event leading to dose reduction or discontinuation during the first cycle of treatment.
RESULTS: We enrolled 277 patients: 76% had metastatic disease; 89% received chemotherapy and 11% targeted therapy; 29% were normometabolic, 51% hypermetabolic and 20% hypometabolic. Fifty-nine patients (21%) experienced an ELT. Toxicity was associated with abnormal metabolism (vs normal: OR = 2.37 [1.13-4.94], p = 0.023), PS (2-3 vs 0-1: OR = 2.04 [1.12-3.74], p = 0.023), albumin (<35 vs ≥35 g/l: OR = 2.39 [1.03-5.54], p = 0.048), and inflammation (CRP ≥10 vs <10 mg/l: OR = 2.43 [1.35-4.38], p = 0.004). To predict toxicity, the most sensitive parameter was the REE (83%) followed by PINI (63%), GPS (59%), CRP (55%), PS (41%), NRI (37%), and albumin (16%). In multivariate analysis, elevated CRP was an independent predictor of toxicity (p = 0.047).
CONCLUSION: Abnormal basal energy metabolism identifies patients at higher risk of treatment-related acute complications.

sources.title: Bone metastases induce metabolic changes and mitophagy in mice.
sources.authors: Jenna Wilcox-Hagerty, Haifang Xu, Brian A Hain, Amy C Arnold, David L Waning
sources.abstract:
NEW FINDINGS: What is the central question of this study? Cachexia causes severe changes in skeletal muscle metabolism and function and is a key predictor of negative outcomes in cancer patients: what are the changes in whole animal energy metabolism and mitochondria in skeletal muscle? What is the main finding and its importance? There is decreased whole animal energy expenditure in mice with cachexia. They displayed highly dysmorphic mitochondria and mitophagy in skeletal muscle.
ABSTRACT: Cachexia causes changes in skeletal muscle metabolism. Mice with MDA-MB-231 breast cancer bone metastases and cachexia have decreased whole animal energy metabolism and increased skeletal muscle mitophagy. We examined whole animal energy metabolism by indirect calorimetry in mice with MDA-MB-231 breast cancer bone metastases, and showed decreased energy expenditure. We also examined skeletal muscle mitochondria and found that mitochondria in mice with MDA-MB-231 bone metastases are highly dysmorphic and have altered protein markers of mitochondrial biogenesis and dynamics. In addition, LC3B protein was increased in mitochondria of skeletal muscle from cachectic mice, and colocalized with the mitochondrial protein Tom20. Our data demonstrate the importance of mitophagy in cachexia. Understanding these changes will help contribute to defining treatments for cancer cachexia.

drafts:
### Direct Answer
When individualized indirect calorimetry is unavailable, standard oncology nutrition guidance recommends estimating total energy expenditure at **25 to 30 kcal/kg/day** and protein intake at **above 1.0 g/kg/day**, targeting up to **1.5 g/kg/day** when feasible [S01]. 

For a 60 kg adult with cancer (without severe renal impairment, fluid retention, or refeeding risk):
* **Daily Energy Target:** **1,500 to 1,800 kcal/day**
* **Daily Protein Target:** **> 60 g/day up to 90 g/day**

---

### Step-by-Step Arithmetic

1. **Energy Calculation:**
   $$\text{Lower boundary: } 60\text{ kg} \times 25\text{ kcal/kg/day} = 1,500\text{ kcal/day}$$
   $$\text{Upper boundary: } 60\text{ kg} \times 30\text{ kcal/kg/day} = 1,800\text{ kcal/day}$$
   *Target range: 1,500–1,800 kcal/day* [S01].

2. **Protein Calculation:**
   $$\text{Baseline target: } > 1.0\text{ g/kg/day} \times 60\text{ kg} = > 60\text{ g/day}$$
   $$\text{Upper target: } 1.5\text{ g/kg/day} \times 60\text{ kg} = 90\text{ g/day}$$
   *Target range: approximately 60 to 90 g/day* [S01].

---

### Rationale and Practical Considerations
* **Energy Needs:** The 25–30 kcal/kg/day range provides a baseline maintenance estimate for ambulatory or bedridden patients with standard activity levels [S01]. 
* **Protein Needs:** Patients with cancer experience increased protein breakdown driven by systemic inflammation and tumor-host interactions. Aiming above 1.0 g/kg/day and up to 1.5 g/kg/day helps counteract muscle catabolism and preserve fat-free mass [S01].
* **Nutritional Route:** When oral intake falls short despite nutritional counseling and oral nutritional supplements, enteral support should be considered before parenteral nutrition, provided the gastrointestinal tract is functional [S01].

---

### Limitations of Rule-of-Thumb Weight-Based Targets
Weight-based rule-of-thumb formulas serve only as starting approximations and have several important limitations:

1. **Metabolic Heterogeneity:** Cancer populations exhibit wide variability in resting energy expenditure (REE). Studies measuring REE by indirect calorimetry demonstrate that cancer patients can be hypermetabolic, normometabolic, or hypometabolic depending on tumor type, stage, and systemic inflammation (such as acute-phase reactant elevations like C-reactive protein) [P18359195, P19647909, P28143668]. Standard predictive formulas frequently show poor agreement with measured energy expenditure in patients with active malignancy [P18359195].
2. **Body Composition vs. Total Weight:** Using actual body weight assumes normal body composition. It does not account for sarcopenia, sarcopenic obesity, or unmeasured shifts in fat-free mass versus extracellular water [P19647909]. Without height to calculate body mass index (BMI), whether 60 kg represents underweight, normal weight, or post-weight-loss baseline remains unknown [S01].
3. **Clinical Trajectory and Context:** 
   * **Cancer Cachexia:** Cachexia is a driven metabolic syndrome involving systemic inflammation and muscle wasting that cannot be reversed by calorie loading alone [S02, S09]. 
   * **Intestinal Failure vs. End-of-Life:** In severe mechanical obstruction or gut failure, specialized artificial nutrition decisions are required [S09]. Conversely, in terminal stages near the end of life, full nutritional targets are inappropriate, and care shifts strictly to comfort and symptom relief [S09].
4. **Refeeding Caveat:** Although refeeding risk was excluded in this synthetic profile, patients with prolonged starvation or rapid, profound weight loss must never receive full maintenance targets immediately; they require cautious ramp-up with electrolyte and thiamine support [S04].

*Note: This information is for educational discussion and does not constitute a personalized clinical prescription.*

reviews.uncertainty_note: Rule-of-thumb weight-based targets (25-30 kcal/kg/day for energy, 1.0-1.5 g/kg/day for protein) provide pragmatic starting estimates, but resting metabolic rate varies widely across cancer types, stages, and inflammatory states, and weight alone does not reflect true fat-free mass.

sources.abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Alterations of nutritional and performance status (PS) are associated with higher risk of chemotherapy toxicity. Increased resting energy expenditure (REE) is frequent in cancer patients and may contribute to cachexia. We investigated whether abnormal energetic metabolism could predict early acute limiting toxicities (ELT) of anticancer treatments.
METHODS: In this observational monocentric study, REE was measured by indirect calorimetry before treatment initiation. Based on the ratio of measured REE to REE predicted by the Harris-Benedict formula, patients were classified as hypometabolic (<90%), normometabolic (90-110%) or hypermetabolic (>110%). Body mass index, weight loss, PS, albumin, transthyretin, C-reactive protein (CRP) and muscle mass (CT-scan) were studied. Were defined as ELT any unplanned hospitalization or any adverse event leading to dose reduction or discontinuation during the first cycle of treatment.
RESULTS: We enrolled 277 patients: 76% had metastatic disease; 89% received chemotherapy and 11% targeted therapy; 29% were normometabolic, 51% hypermetabolic and 20% hypometabolic. Fifty-nine patients (21%) experienced an ELT. Toxicity was associated with abnormal metabolism (vs normal: OR = 2.37 [1.13-4.94], p = 0.023), PS (2-3 vs 0-1: OR = 2.04 [1.12-3.74], p = 0.023), albumin (<35 vs ≥35 g/l: OR = 2.39 [1.03-5.54], p = 0.048), and inflammation (CRP ≥10 vs <10 mg/l: OR = 2.43 [1.35-4.38], p = 0.004). To predict toxicity, the most sensitive parameter was the REE (83%) followed by PINI (63%), GPS (59%), CRP (55%), PS (41%), NRI (37%), and albumin (16%). In multivariate analysis, elevated CRP was an independent predictor of toxicity (p = 0.047).
CONCLUSION: Abnormal basal energy metabolism identifies patients at higher risk of treatment-related acute complications.

### Direct Answer
When individualized indirect calorimetry is unavailable, standard oncology nutrition guidance recommends estimating total energy expenditure at **25 to 30 kcal/kg/day** and protein intake at **above 1.0 g/kg/day**, targeting up to **1.5 g/kg/day** when feasible [S01]. 

For a 60 kg adult with cancer (without severe renal impairment, fluid retention, or refeeding risk):
* **Daily Energy Target:** **1,500 to 1,800 kcal/day**
* **Daily Protein Target:** **> 60 g/day up to 90 g/day**

---

### Step-by-Step Arithmetic

1. **Energy Calculation:**
   $$\text{Lower boundary: } 60\text{ kg} \times 25\text{ kcal/kg/day} = 1,500\text{ kcal/day}$$
   $$\text{Upper boundary: } 60\text{ kg} \times 30\text{ kcal/kg/day} = 1,800\text{ kcal/day}$$
   *Target range: 1,500–1,800 kcal/day* [S01].

2. **Protein Calculation:**
   $$\text{Baseline target: } > 1.0\text{ g/kg/day} \times 60\text{ kg} = > 60\text{ g/day}$$
   $$\text{Upper target: } 1.5\text{ g/kg/day} \times 60\text{ kg} = 90\text{ g/day}$$
   *Target range: approximately 60 to 90 g/day* [S01].

---

### Rationale and Practical Considerations
* **Energy Needs:** The 25–30 kcal/kg/day range provides a baseline maintenance estimate for ambulatory or bedridden patients with standard activity levels [S01]. 
* **Protein Needs:** Patients with cancer experience increased protein breakdown driven by systemic inflammation and tumor-host interactions. Aiming above 1.0 g/kg/day and up to 1.5 g/kg/day helps counteract muscle catabolism and preserve fat-free mass [S01].
* **Nutritional Route:** When oral intake falls short despite nutritional counseling and oral nutritional supplements, enteral support should be considered before parenteral nutrition, provided the gastrointestinal tract is functional [S01].

---

### Limitations of Rule-of-Thumb Weight-Based Targets
Weight-based rule-of-thumb formulas serve only as starting approximations and have several important limitations:

1. **Metabolic Heterogeneity:** Cancer populations exhibit wide variability in resting energy expenditure (REE). Studies measuring REE by indirect calorimetry demonstrate that cancer patients can be hypermetabolic, normometabolic, or hypometabolic depending on tumor type, stage, and systemic inflammation (such as acute-phase reactant elevations like C-reactive protein) [P18359195, P19647909, P28143668]. Standard predictive formulas frequently show poor agreement with measured energy expenditure in patients with active malignancy [P18359195].
2. **Body Composition vs. Total Weight:** Using actual body weight assumes normal body composition. It does not account for sarcopenia, sarcopenic obesity, or unmeasured shifts in fat-free mass versus extracellular water [P19647909]. Without height to calculate body mass index (BMI), whether 60 kg represents underweight, normal weight, or post-weight-loss baseline remains unknown [S01].
3. **Clinical Trajectory and Context:** 
   * **Cancer Cachexia:** Cachexia is a driven metabolic syndrome involving systemic inflammation and muscle wasting that cannot be reversed by calorie loading alone [S02, S09]. 
   * **Intestinal Failure vs. End-of-Life:** In severe mechanical obstruction or gut failure, specialized artificial nutrition decisions are required [S09]. Conversely, in terminal stages near the end of life, full nutritional targets are inappropriate, and care shifts strictly to comfort and symptom relief [S09].
4. **Refeeding Caveat:** Although refeeding risk was excluded in this synthetic profile, patients with prolonged starvation or rapid, profound weight loss must never receive full maintenance targets immediately; they require cautious ramp-up with electrolyte and thiamine support [S04].

*Note: This information is for educational discussion and does not constitute a personalized clinical prescription.*
